consensus_summary: Lamp oil is primarily the Holy Spirit (indwelling presence, empowering and illuminating grace that sustains spiritual light), drawn from Zechariah 4, anointing texts, tabernacle lamp oil, and popular readings of the Ten Virgins; secondary alternatives include genuine faith/grace, good works/charity, readiness, or the Word.
book_summary: The commandment's truth and correction received and laid up inwardly until they govern the life—the tested, pressed fruit of the Spirit stored as proven obedience; light is that obedience made visible as an example to others.
book_core_identification: inwardly laid-up commandment truth/correction yielding proven obedience (pressed fruit of the Spirit)
boundary_disagreement: Book demotes the Spirit identification to a mere common teaching and reassigns oil to the stored product (obedience/truth) rather than the Spirit Himself, thereby excluding pure-Spirit cases while retaining only those mediated by internalized commandments.
material_contradiction: Oil cannot simultaneously be the Holy Spirit and the fruit of the Spirit (proven obedience to commandments) as the same referent; the book requires rejecting the consensus identification even while noting causal linkage via the Spirit.
rationale: Consensus responses uniformly core on the Holy Spirit as primary (with high confidence and shared bases in Zech 4, anointing, and Matt 25), treating faith/works/readiness/Word as secondary. The book explicitly flags the Spirit view as common yet advances a distinct core of stored commandments producing obedience as the oil that fuels visible light/good works. Source and product remain different referents; this is replacement, not boundary refinement of the same category, though some secondary alternatives (Word, works) partially overlap the book's cases.
strongest_objection: Zechariah 4:6–14 explicitly ties the oil feeding the lampstand to 'my Spirit,' supplying direct textual warrant for the consensus core that the book sets aside.
